glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: Proverbs 10 opens Solomon’s collection of short sayings by carrying the two ways into the home, the harvest field, the purse, and the mouth, showing that the righteous rest on a lasting foundation while the way of the wicked passes away.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Wisdom and Folly have just issued their rival invitations (9:1–18). A new heading, “The proverbs of Solomon” (10:1), now turns the book from long appeals to short two-line sayings, most of them sharp contrasts.

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “The mouth of the righteous is a well of life, But violence covers the mouth of the wicked.” (Proverbs 10:11)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
With chapter 10 the father’s long appeals give way to single sayings, and the first one goes straight back into the home: “A wise son makes a glad father, But a foolish son is the grief of his mother” (10:1). The choice between wisdom and folly that filled chapters 1–9 now shows up in ordinary places. A son who sleeps through harvest shames his family (10:5), and the lazy man is like “smoke to the eyes” to those who send him (10:26).

The largest cluster concerns speech. Twice the chapter says that “violence covers the mouth of the wicked” (10:6, 11), words that hide the harm in a heart, while the mouth of the righteous is “a well of life.” Righteous lips are “choice silver” and “feed many” (10:20–21), but hidden hatred, slander, and “the multitude of words” open the door to sin (10:18–19).

Behind the contrasts stands the LORD Himself. He will not let the righteous soul famish (10:3), His blessing makes rich without sorrow (10:22), and His way is “strength for the upright” (10:29). These are general truths about God’s ordered world rather than promises for every case, yet they show plainly that God is not neutral between the two ways. When the whirlwind passes, the wicked are gone, “But the righteous has an everlasting foundation” (10:25).

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Proverbs 10:1–5 — A Wise Son and Diligent Hands

Under Solomon’s name, the first saying ties a son’s choices to his parents’ gladness or grief, and the sayings that follow show what is at stake: wicked gain cannot rescue from death, the LORD sustains the righteous, and work done or neglected at harvest brings a family plenty or shame. Diligence is commended as wisdom at work, without blaming those who are poor through hardship or inability.

Proverbs 10:6–11 — Blessing on the Righteous, Violence in the Mouth of the Wicked

A repeated line about violence covering the mouth of the wicked frames sayings on how a life is remembered, how it stands, and how it speaks. The teachable heart and the person of integrity walk securely, while the chattering fool and the one who winks to make mischief fall or are found out, and the section closes with the righteous mouth as a well of life.

Proverbs 10:12–21 — Words That Wound and Words That Feed

These sayings weigh the moral value of words and what lies behind them: love refuses to keep a quarrel burning, the wise store up knowledge until it is needed, and restrained lips guard against sin, while hidden hatred, slander, and careless talk bring ruin. Woven among them are reminders that wealth, wages, and the response to correction all lead somewhere, and the section ends with the righteous feeding many by what they say.

Proverbs 10:22–30 — The Everlasting Foundation of the Righteous

The LORD’s blessing, the delights of the fool and the wise, and the fears and hopes of each are traced to their ends: the wicked meet what they dread and vanish like debris in a storm, while the hope of the righteous turns to gladness and they stand on a foundation that lasts. Read as general truths, these sayings describe how the two ways finally end without promising the righteous a life free of loss or explaining every early death.

Proverbs 10:31–32 — The Mouth of the Righteous Brings Forth Wisdom

The chapter closes as it has run, with the mouth. Righteous lips bear wisdom like fruit and know what is fitting to say, while the twisted tongue that knows only what is perverse will be cut out.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Proverbs 10 teaches how to read the rest of Solomon’s sayings. Each verse sets two lines side by side, so the reader learns to recognize the two ways of chapters 1–9 in a harvest field, an honest wage, or a single remark. The outcome sayings describe how God’s world generally works and how the two ways finally end, and they are never grounds for blaming the poor, the grieving, or a family that has buried someone young (10:3, 27, 30).

The chapter also gives speech great moral weight. The same mouth can be a well of life or a cover for violence. When Solomon says “love covers all sins” (10:12), and Peter takes up the thought for the church (1 Peter 4:8), love refuses to keep a conflict alive, though it never means hiding abuse or avoiding needed correction.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
Two ways in daily life. Nearly every verse sets the righteous against the wicked or the wise against the foolish, carrying the two ways into family, work, and money (10:1–5, 15–16, 24–25).

The mouth and the heart. Speech gives life or hides violence, and it reveals what fills the heart (10:6, 11, 13–14, 18–21, 31–32).

Diligence and laziness. The diligent hand and the son who gathers in summer stand against the slack hand, the sleeper in harvest, and the lazy man who frustrates those who depend on him (10:4–5, 26).

The LORD behind the outcomes. God sustains the righteous, gives the blessing that makes rich, and makes His way strength for the upright and destruction for evildoers (10:3, 22, 27, 29).

What lasts. The memory, hope, and foundation of the righteous endure, while the name, expectation, and place of the wicked perish (10:7, 25, 28, 30).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
The proverbs of Solomon (10:1). The heading that begins the first collection of short sayings, which runs to 22:16. Its sayings are grouped by repeated words and subjects, so they reward reading in clusters.

The righteous and the wicked (10:3, 6–7, 24–25, 28–32). Righteousness in Proverbs is a way of life before God, rooted in the fear of the LORD; the wicked walk the opposite way. These two names mark the broad division beneath every other character type in the book.

A prating fool (10:8, 10). One who chatters without listening. The fool in Proverbs is morally deficient rather than slow, and his own talking keeps him from hearing the instruction that would keep him standing.

The lazy man (10:26). The NKJV’s term here for the sluggard first portrayed in 6:6–11. Proverbs distinguishes laziness from inability, illness, or genuine need.

The blessing of the LORD (10:22). Riches that come as God’s gift, without the sorrow that grasping or ill-gotten wealth brings. Some translators render the second line to say that toil adds nothing to it; either way the LORD is the source, and the verse is no formula for wealth.

The fear of the LORD (10:27). A right view of God: terror for those who defy Him and awe for all at His glory, majesty, and holiness, for He is unlike any other. It tends to lengthen life, a general pattern and not a rule that explains every early death.

1.brief: A new heading, “The proverbs of Solomon,” opens the first collection of short sayings, and the first one returns to the home of the prologue. A wise son makes his father glad, while a foolish son brings grief to his mother, so the path a son chooses is felt by the whole family.
1.explain:
“The proverbs of Solomon:”

This is the first new heading since 1:1, and it changes the form of the book. The long speeches of the father and of Wisdom give way to short sayings, most only two lines long. This first collection runs to 22:16. In chapter 10 nearly every saying is a contrast: the second line, usually beginning with “But,” sets its picture against the first. The reader learns to read the two lines against each other, asking what each side shows about the other. The sayings are still part of the same book. They carry the two ways of chapters 1–9 into the home, the field, the market, and the mouth, and they are grouped by repeated words and subjects rather than thrown together at random.

“A wise son makes a glad father,”

The first saying goes straight back into the home of the prologue, where a father spoke to “my son.” Wisdom and folly are never private matters. A son who walks wisely brings real gladness to his father.

“But a foolish son is the grief of his mother.”

The contrast is grief, a heavy and lasting sorrow. The foolish son in Proverbs is not slow of mind; he is morally careless and despises instruction. Hebrew poetry often spreads one thought across both lines, so the point is not that only fathers rejoice and only mothers grieve. Both parents share both outcomes, just as both were honored in the father’s first appeal: “hear the instruction of your father, And do not forsake the law of your mother” (1:8). The path a son chooses is felt by the whole household.
1.notes:
The collection that begins here runs from 10:1 to 22:16 and contains 375 verses in the NKJV numbering.

The first line of 15:20 repeats the first line of this verse word for word in Hebrew, “A wise son makes a father glad,” and 17:25 returns to the grief a foolish son brings to his parents.

2.brief: Wealth gained by wickedness may look like security, but it profits nothing in the end. Righteousness, by contrast, delivers from death, which is something no treasure can do.
2.explain:
“Treasures of wickedness profit nothing,”

These are riches gained by wicked means: theft, fraud, oppression, and violence. The gang of 1:10–19 promised exactly this kind of treasure: “We shall fill our houses with spoil” (1:13). Such wealth looks like security, and it can buy a great deal, but when life itself is at stake it profits nothing.

“But righteousness delivers from death.”

Righteousness, living rightly before God, does what no treasure can do. In the setting of Proverbs, the wicked way leads to an early and violent end; the gang that grasped for gain was lying in wait “for their own blood” (1:18). Righteousness keeps a person off that road and out of that end. The verse does not explain how deliverance comes in every case, and Proverbs speaks here in its usual general terms. Its contrast is still sharp: one kind of gain cannot save a life, and the other preserves it. Placed right after the first saying, it shows what a wise son is choosing when he refuses wicked gain.
2.notes: The second line is repeated word for word in 11:4, where it answers a different first line: “Riches do not profit in the day of wrath.”

3.brief: The LORD Himself stands behind the contrast: He will not let the righteous starve, and He pushes away what the wicked crave. This is a general truth about God’s care and His opposition to evil, not a promise that a righteous person will never know want.
3.explain:
“The LORD will not allow the righteous soul to famish,”

This is the first time the LORD is named in Solomon’s collection, and He stands behind the contrast between the two ways. The “soul” here is the whole living person, including the appetite and its need for food. To “famish” is to go hungry. The LORD cares for the righteous and provides for them. This is a general truth about God’s care, not a promise that a righteous person will never know want. Faithful people in Scripture have gone hungry; Paul could describe his ministry as lived “in hunger and thirst” (2 Corinthians 11:27).

“But He casts away the desire of the wicked.”

The wicked crave, and the LORD thrusts their craving aside. What they reach for, He does not allow them to secure. The verse shows that God is not neutral between the two ways. He sustains the one and resists the other, which is why “Treasures of wickedness profit nothing” in the end (10:2).
3.notes:
The Hebrew word translated “soul” can refer to the appetite as well as to the whole living person, which fits the image of going hungry.

The Hebrew word behind “desire” in the second line is difficult because it has two quite different meanings. It can mean a craving, usually a bad one, or it can mean ruin and destruction. Brown-Driver-Briggs places this verse under the first meaning, and the ESV agrees with “craving.” The KJV has “substance,” and the 1611 edition offers in its margin an alternative rendering that speaks of the wicked being cast away for their wickedness. The NKJV’s “desire” follows the sense of craving: the LORD pushes aside what the wicked long for.

4.brief: Work habits have consequences: a slack, careless hand leads to poverty, while the diligent hand produces wealth. The saying commends diligence as wisdom applied to work and describes the usual result rather than a formula for riches, and it does not blame those who are poor through inability or hardship.
4.explain:
“He who has a slack hand becomes poor,”

The hand stands for a person’s work. A slack hand is loose, careless, and negligent; it does the job halfway or not at all. Over time such habits lead to poverty. Proverbs treats this as one of the plain patterns of life in God’s world.

“But the hand of the diligent makes rich.”

The diligent person works with focus and steady effort, and the usual result is plenty. This is wisdom applied to work, the skill of doing the right thing with care and persistence. The saying describes how work generally pays; it is not a formula that guarantees riches. Nor does it blame everyone who is poor. Proverbs itself knows that poverty can come from injustice: “Much food is in the fallow ground of the poor, And for lack of justice there is waste” (13:23). This verse addresses the poverty that comes from neglect, and it calls the reader to diligent hands. It also prepares for 10:22, where the same verb, “makes rich,” describes the blessing of the LORD.
4.notes: The Hebrew word for “the diligent” returns in 12:24, 13:4, and 21:5, each time set against the lazy or the hasty, so this verse begins a thread the collection keeps following.

5.brief: The harvest season makes the contrast concrete. The son who gathers while the crops are ready is wise, but the one who sleeps through harvest brings shame on his family; he is the lazy man of 6:6–11, missing a moment that will not come again.
5.explain:
“He who gathers in summer is a wise son;”

In Israel the summer months brought the harvest of grain and fruit, the season when the year’s food had to be gathered. The son who works then is called wise, the same description used in 10:1. Here wisdom is a matter of timing: doing the work while the season is open. He is like the ant, which “Provides her supplies in the summer” (6:8).

“He who sleeps in harvest is a son who causes shame.”

The other son sleeps through the harvest. He is the lazy man of 6:6–11, whose motto is “A little sleep, a little slumber” (6:10). The harvest does not wait for him; when the season passes, the opportunity is gone and the family goes short. His laziness is not only his own loss. He brings shame on his household, the same kind of shame and grief the first verse described. Together 10:1 and 10:5 frame the opening section with a wise son and a foolish one.
5.notes:
The phrase “a son who causes shame” translates the same Hebrew wording in 17:2 and 19:26.

Proverbs 10:6–11 — Blessing on the Righteous, Violence in the Mouth of the Wicked

6.brief: Blessings rest on the head of the righteous like a crown, openly given and received. The mouth of the wicked, however, is covered by violence, his speech hiding the harm in his heart, and the line returns in verse 11 to frame this section.
6.explain:
“Blessings are on the head of the righteous,”

In Scripture a blessing was often pictured as resting on the head, as when Jacob laid his hands on the heads of Joseph’s sons (Genesis 48:14) and spoke of blessings “on the head of Joseph” (Genesis 49:26). The righteous wear their blessings openly. Good gifts from God, and the goodwill of others, rest on them where everyone can see.

“But violence covers the mouth of the wicked.”

The Hebrew is compact and can be read two ways. It may mean that the mouth of the wicked conceals violence, his speech covering the harm he intends, or that his own violence finally covers his mouth and silences him. The NKJV keeps the wording open. In this verse the contrast of head and mouth points to the first sense: what rests on the righteous is blessing, while what lies behind the words of the wicked is violence. The same line returns in 10:11, framing the section with two sayings about the mouth of the wicked.
6.notes:
The ESV and NASB take the first sense, saying that the mouth of the wicked “conceals violence,” and the NLT reads “the words of the wicked conceal violent intentions.” The 1984 NIV takes the other sense, “violence overwhelms.”

The Hebrew verb behind “covers” is a catchword in this part of the chapter, a repeated word that links neighboring sayings. It recurs in 10:11, in “love covers all sins” (10:12), and in “Whoever hides hatred” (10:18), where the NKJV translates it “hides.” Following the word through these verses shows the same act of covering put to opposite uses: the wicked cover violence, love covers sins, and the liar covers hatred.

7.brief: The contrast reaches past death. The righteous are remembered with blessing and their names spoken with gratitude, but the name of the wicked rots like something dead until no one wants to say it.
7.explain:
“The memory of the righteous is blessed,”

The contrast now reaches beyond death. When the righteous are gone, they are remembered with blessing. People speak their names with gratitude, and their memory continues to do good. The blessings that rested on their heads in life (10:6) carry on in the way they are remembered.

“But the name of the wicked will rot.”

A name in Scripture is a person’s reputation and the memory of who he was. The name of the wicked rots like something dead, decaying until no one wants to speak it. The picture is vivid and unpleasant on purpose. Whatever the wicked gained or built, what remains of him spoils. The verse calls the reader to think about what a life leaves behind.
7.notes:
The Hebrew of the first line reads literally, the memory of the righteous is for a blessing, and the ESV renders it “a blessing.” The wording suggests that the memory of the righteous becomes a blessing to others, not only that it is spoken of well.

The Hebrew verb “rot” is related to the noun translated “rottenness” in 12:4 and 14:30, where it describes decay in the bones. The same picture of slow decay lies behind what happens to the name of the wicked here.

8.brief: A wise heart is teachable and receives commands, while “a prating fool,” one who chatters without listening, will fall. His own talking keeps him from hearing the instruction that would have kept him standing.
8.explain:
“The wise in heart will receive commands,”

The wise in heart are wise inwardly, not merely in appearance. Their wisdom shows in teachability: they receive commands. They listen, take instruction, and let it direct them. Wisdom begins with receiving before it begins with speaking.

“But a prating fool will fall.”

A “prating fool” is a chatterer; the Hebrew says literally a fool of lips. He talks so much that he never listens, so the instruction that could have kept him upright never reaches him. He “will fall,” brought down by his own folly. The contrast is between the heart and the lips, between receiving and talking. The line is repeated at 10:10.
8.notes: The 1611 King James Version notes in its margin that the Hebrew behind “a prating fool” is literally a fool of lips. Its second note offers be beaten only as an alternative rendering of “fall”; the Hebrew verb means to be thrown or thrust down. The ESV calls him “babbling.”

9.brief: Integrity gives a person secure footing, because he has nothing to hide and no fear of being found out. The one who twists his ways may get by for a while, but he will become known, because crooked paths are eventually exposed.
9.explain:
“He who walks with integrity walks securely,”

Integrity is wholeness, a life without a hidden side. The person who walks with integrity walks with confidence, because he has nothing to cover up and no fear of being found out. His security does not come from cleverness or luck but from the plainness of his ways.

“But he who perverts his ways will become known.”

The one who twists his ways, bending them toward deceit, may get by for a time, but he “will become known.” Crooked paths are eventually exposed. Moses warned Israel in Numbers 32:23, “be sure your sin will find you out.” The contrast is between living securely and living in danger of exposure. Integrity is not only right; it is also the safer way to live.
9.notes: A later saying sets the same pair side by side: “Whoever walks blamelessly will be saved, But he who is perverse in his ways will suddenly fall” (28:18).

10.brief: The one who winks with the eye, signaling mischief behind someone’s back, causes trouble for others. The second line repeats verse 8, linking the sly signaler with the careless talker as two ways of misusing what should communicate truth.
10.explain:
“He who winks with the eye causes trouble,”

The wink here is a secret signal of malice, not a friendly gesture. It says one thing behind what is openly said, a sign between people plotting against someone. The worthless man of 6:12–14 “winks with his eyes” as part of his scheming (6:13), and in Psalm 35:19 David prays, “Nor let them wink with the eye who hate me without a cause.” Such a person causes trouble, pain and grief for others, without ever saying a word that could be held against him.

“But a prating fool will fall.”

The second line repeats 10:8. The sly signaler and the careless talker stand side by side as two ways of misusing what should communicate truth. One harms others quietly; the other ruins himself loudly. Both end badly, and placing the familiar line here invites the reader to compare them.
10.notes:
The NLT’s second line, “but a bold reproof promotes peace,” matches the Greek Septuagint, which in Brenton’s English translation (1851) says that the one who reproves boldly is a peacemaker. The Hebrew text, followed by the NKJV, ESV, and NASB, repeats the second line of 10:8.

Where the NKJV has “But,” the ESV reads “and,” since the Hebrew connective can mean either.

11.brief: Righteous speech is “a well of life,” a spring that refreshes and sustains those who drink from it. The wicked man’s mouth hides violence, as verse 6 already said, and the repeated line closes this section by setting life-giving words against words that cover harm.
11.explain:
“The mouth of the righteous is a well of life,”

A well or spring in a dry land meant life itself. The words of the righteous are like that: a source that refreshes, sustains, and keeps giving to those who draw from it. Proverbs uses the same image for the teaching of the wise and for the fear of the LORD (13:14; 14:27). The God who is “the fountain of life” (Psalm 36:9) makes the speech of His people a source of life to others.

“But violence covers the mouth of the wicked.”

The line from 10:6 returns, now set against a different first line. In 10:6 the contrast was head and mouth; here it is mouth and mouth. The same organ can pour out life or hide violence. The repetition closes the section and points ahead to the next one, where the chapter gathers many sayings about the use of words.
11.notes:
The Hebrew phrase behind “a well of life” is the one the NKJV renders “a fountain of life” in 13:14 and 14:27.

Proverbs 10:12–21 — Words That Wound and Words That Feed

12.brief: Hatred keeps old quarrels alive and stirs up fresh strife, but love covers all sins, refusing to broadcast another’s wrongs and choosing to forgive (1 Peter 4:8). Covering sin in love does not mean hiding abuse or avoiding needed correction, but it does mean refusing to keep a conflict burning.
12.explain:
“Hatred stirs up strife,”

Hatred does not let a quarrel rest. It wakes up old grievances, retells old injuries, and keeps conflict alive. Where hatred lives, strife keeps breaking out again, because hatred wants the offense remembered.

“But love covers all sins.”

Love does the opposite. To cover a sin is to refuse to expose it, broadcast it, or keep bringing it up; it is the choice to forgive and let the offense go. Proverbs says the same elsewhere: “He who covers a transgression seeks love” (17:9). Peter takes up this line for the church: “love will cover a multitude of sins” (1 Peter 4:8). Covering sin in love does not mean concealing abuse or crime, enabling ongoing wrongdoing, or avoiding needed correction. Proverbs also says, “Open rebuke is better Than love carefully concealed” (27:5), and it warns that “He who covers his sins will not prosper” (28:13). The love in this verse covers the offenses of others so that peace can be restored. It does not hide one’s own sin from God or shield wrongdoing from justice.
12.notes: For “all sins” the ESV reads “all offenses.” The Hebrew word is the one often translated transgression, a wrong that breaks faith with another person or rebels against God. It is the same word translated “sin” in 10:19.

13.brief: Wisdom shows up on the lips of the person who understands, so his words carry help to others. The one who lacks understanding will not learn from words and needs the rod on his back, correction he could have avoided by listening.
13.explain:
“Wisdom is found on the lips of him who has understanding,”

Understanding shows up in what a person says. Wisdom can be “found” on his lips, so others who listen to him find help and direction. The understanding person carries wisdom in his words and passes it on.

“But a rod is for the back of him who is devoid of understanding.”

The one “devoid of understanding,” in Hebrew literally lacking heart, is the same kind of person as the young man of 7:7. He will not learn from words, so he learns from the rod. In its setting the rod is the tool of correction, and the saying is plain about the result: what a person refuses to receive through his ears he may have to receive on his back. Proverbs says it again: “a rod for the fool’s back” (26:3). The contrast of lips and back shows that correction will come one way or the other. It is far better to receive it through words.
13.notes: The Hebrew phrase behind “devoid of understanding” is literally lacking heart, the same phrase used in 9:4 and 7:7; the person lacks the inner sense and judgment that the heart stands for in Proverbs. The 1611 King James Version translates the phrase void of understanding and adds the marginal note “Hebr. heart.” That note replaces only the word “understanding” with the Hebrew word heart; the idea of lacking is already in the English text. The same Hebrew expression lies behind “lack of wisdom” in 10:21.

14.brief: The wise store up knowledge like provisions, holding it until the right time to use it. The fool’s mouth works the other way, pouring out whatever he thinks and bringing him close to ruin with every careless word.
14.explain:
“Wise people store up knowledge,”

To store up is to lay something away as a treasure or a provision, kept safe until it is needed. The wise do this with knowledge. They gather it, keep it, and hold it ready for the right moment. They do not need to spend every thought as soon as it comes.

“But the mouth of the foolish is near destruction.”

The fool works the other way. Whatever comes into his head comes out of his mouth, and every careless word brings him a step closer to ruin. Destruction is “near,” close at hand. The contrast is between storing and spending: the wise keep knowledge in reserve, while the fool’s talk is a constant danger to himself.
14.notes:
The Hebrew word for “destruction” is a catchword in this chapter. It appears again in 10:15, “The destruction of the poor,” and in 10:29, “destruction will come to the workers of iniquity.”

The Hebrew verb behind “store up” is the one used in 2:7, where the LORD “stores up sound wisdom for the upright.” It means to hide something away as a treasure. The wise do with knowledge what the LORD does with wisdom: they keep it in reserve until it is needed.

15.brief: Here is a plain observation of life: the rich man’s wealth works like a fortified city around him, while poverty leaves the poor exposed to ruin. The saying describes what money does in a fallen world without praising it, and later Proverbs adds that this fortress is “a high wall in his own esteem” (18:11).
15.explain:
“The rich man’s wealth is his strong city;”

This is a plain observation of life. Wealth works like a fortified city around a rich man. It shields him from many of the troubles that would overwhelm others, such as a bad harvest, a sudden expense, or a strong enemy. The saying describes what money does in a fallen world without praising it.

“The destruction of the poor is their poverty.”

The poor have no such walls. Poverty leaves them exposed, so that a small setback can become ruin. The saying is not admiration of the rich or contempt for the poor; it states how things are. Proverbs later adds an important correction to the first line: “The rich man’s wealth is his strong city, And like a high wall in his own esteem” (18:11). That fortress is partly imagined, and the verse just before it names the only true refuge: “The name of the LORD is a strong tower” (18:10). The book also insists that how a person treats the poor matters to God (14:31).

16.brief: Both the righteous and the wicked work and are paid. The righteous man’s labor serves life, while the wicked man’s earnings only feed more sin, so the direction of a person’s gain matters more than its size.
16.explain:
“The labor of the righteous leads to life,”

Both the righteous and the wicked work and are paid. The labor of the righteous, the earnings that come from his work, serves life. It sustains his household, supplies others, and supports the way of life. His gain stays in the service of what is good.

“The wages of the wicked to sin.”

The wicked man earns too, but his earnings only feed more sin. What he gains, he spends on the way of death. The saying does not condemn wealth or wages as such; it looks at where each person’s gain goes. The direction of a person’s income matters more than its size. This saying follows naturally from the observation about wealth and poverty in 10:15, which described what money does; this one asks where it goes.
16.notes: The two lines use different Hebrew nouns. The first means work or the wages that work earns; the second means produce or yield, a word often used of crops and income. The ESV distinguishes them as “wage” and “gain,” and the KJV as “labour” and “fruit.”

17.brief: Keeping instruction places a person on “the way of life.” Whoever refuses correction leaves that road and goes astray, so how a person answers correction decides which way he walks.
17.explain:
“He who keeps instruction is in the way of life,”

To keep instruction is to hold on to it and guard it, not just to hear it once. The instruction in view is discipline and correction, the training that keeps a person on course. Whoever keeps it is already walking “in the way of life.” Proverbs said earlier, “Reproofs of instruction are the way of life” (6:23). Correction is part of the road to life, not a detour from it.

“But he who refuses correction goes astray.”

The one who refuses correction throws away the very thing that would keep him on the road. He wanders off. The Hebrew verb is in a form that usually means causing someone else to wander, so the line may also mean that he leads others astray: the person who will not be corrected can take others with him. Either way, a person’s response to correction decides which way he walks.
17.notes: The Hebrew verb at the end of the verse is in a causative form, which usually means to make someone else wander or to mislead. The 1611 King James Version reads “erreth” and gives causeth to err in its margin as an alternative. The ESV takes the causative sense, saying that he leads others astray, while the NKJV and NASB read “goes astray.”

18.brief: Two sins of speech are set side by side. Hiding hatred behind a friendly face makes a man a liar, and spreading slander makes him a fool; whether hatred is concealed or broadcast, the tongue becomes its tool.
18.explain:
“Whoever hides hatred has lying lips,”

Unlike most sayings in this chapter, this verse is not a contrast; both lines condemn. The first describes the person who covers hatred with friendly words. His lips say one thing while his heart holds another, and that makes him a liar. A later saying describes him: “He who hates, disguises it with his lips, And lays up deceit within himself” (26:24).

“And whoever spreads slander is a fool.”

The second line describes the opposite approach. This person does not hide his hatred; he spreads it, putting out damaging reports about others. Proverbs calls him a fool, because slander harms the speaker as well as the one he speaks against. Whether hatred is concealed behind flattery or broadcast in slander, the tongue becomes its tool. There is no safe way to carry hatred.
18.notes: The verb “hides” is the same Hebrew verb translated “covers” in 10:12. Love covers sins and makes peace; here hatred is covered so that it can work in secret.

19.brief: Many words leave room for sin to slip in, and the more a person talks, the more likely he is to say what he should not. Wisdom shows itself in restraint, the ability to hold one’s lips in check, though the righteous mouth also speaks wisdom when it should (verse 31).
19.explain:
“In the multitude of words sin is not lacking,”

The more a person talks, the more room there is for sin to slip in: exaggeration, gossip, boasting, careless promises, and hurtful remarks. Many words do not make a person sinful, but they do multiply the opportunities. Ecclesiastes says something similar: “a fool’s voice is known by his many words” (Ecclesiastes 5:3).

“But he who restrains his lips is wise.”

To restrain the lips is to hold them back and keep them in check. The wise person knows when not to speak. This is not a rule that silence is always wise. In this same chapter the mouth of the righteous is “a well of life” (10:11) and “brings forth wisdom” (10:31), and his lips “feed many” (10:21). The wisdom here is self-control in speech, saying what should be said and leaving unsaid what should not.
19.notes: The Hebrew verb behind “restrains” is the same verb translated “spares” in 17:27, “He who has knowledge spares his words.”

20.brief: The speech of the righteous is valuable, like “choice silver” refined and pure. The heart of the wicked is worth little, and since the heart is the source of speech, its words are worth little too.
20.explain:
“The tongue of the righteous is choice silver;”

Choice silver is refined silver, purified until the dross is gone. The speech of the righteous has that kind of worth. It is valuable, tested, and pure. What they say is worth hearing because it comes from a life that has been purified.

“The heart of the wicked is worth little.”

The contrast is surprising. The first line speaks of the tongue of the righteous, the second of the heart of the wicked. Even the outward speech of the righteous is worth more than the inward core of the wicked. Since the heart is the source of speech, “For out of it spring the issues of life” (4:23), the words that come from a heart worth little are worth little too.
20.notes: The Hebrew of “worth little” is literally like a little, meaning next to nothing.

21.brief: With their lips the righteous feed many, giving guidance and encouragement that nourish others. Fools cannot even sustain themselves; they die for lack of the very wisdom the righteous share so freely.
21.explain:
“The lips of the righteous feed many,”

The Hebrew verb behind “feed” is the word for a shepherd pasturing his flock. The righteous use their lips the way a shepherd uses pasture. Their words guide, nourish, and sustain many people, not only themselves. Good counsel, encouragement, and truth spoken at the right time are food for others.

“But fools die for lack of wisdom.”

The irony is sharp. The righteous feed many, but fools cannot even feed themselves. They “die for lack of wisdom,” in Hebrew literally for lack of heart. They perish for want of the very thing the righteous share so freely. With this saying the section on speech closes: the right use of words gives life to many, and the lack of wisdom brings death.
21.notes:
The verb “feed” is the same Hebrew verb behind “shepherd” in Psalm 23:1, “The LORD is my shepherd.”

Where the NKJV has “lack of wisdom,” the Hebrew says literally lack of heart, the same expression noted at 10:13. The 1611 King James Version reads for want of wisdom and marks “of heart” in its margin as the Hebrew wording, so the note replaces only “of wisdom.”

Proverbs 10:22–30 — The Everlasting Foundation of the Righteous

22.brief: Real riches come as a gift: “The blessing of the LORD makes one rich.” What He gives comes without the sorrow that grasping or ill-gotten wealth brings, and read with the rest of Proverbs, the saying names the LORD as the source of true blessing rather than promising wealth to all who serve Him.
22.explain:
“The blessing of the LORD makes one rich,”

This saying names the source of true riches. The same verb, “makes rich,” described the diligent hand in 10:4. Diligence matters, but it works under the blessing of the LORD; He is the One who finally gives. The book also warns against trusting in riches: “He who trusts in his riches will fall” (11:28). So this verse is not a formula that promises wealth to everyone who serves God. God promises to meet the needs of His people, and His blessing takes many forms. What the verse insists on is that every good gift comes from Him.

“And He adds no sorrow with it.”

What the LORD gives comes without the sorrow that grasping or ill-gotten wealth brings. Riches gained by greed bring anxiety, conflict, and loss; greed “takes away the life of its owners” (1:19). Proverbs says later, “Better is a little with the fear of the LORD, Than great treasure with trouble” (15:16). The LORD’s gifts do not carry that hidden cost. Some translators read the line differently, as saying that toil adds nothing to it, because the Hebrew word for “sorrow” can also mean painful labor. Either way, the LORD is the source, and His blessing is not something human strain can produce.
22.notes:
The Hebrew of the second line can be read with “sorrow” as the object (“He adds no sorrow”) or as the subject (painful toil adds nothing). The NKJV, ESV, NASB, and NLT take the first reading.

The Hebrew word translated “sorrow” here is the same word used in Genesis 3:16, “In pain you shall bring forth children,” and it is closely related to the words for “sorrow” in that verse and “toil” in Genesis 3:17. The word covers both pain and painful labor. That range explains why the second line can be read either as no sorrow added by the LORD or as human toil adding nothing to His blessing.

23.brief: A fool treats doing evil like a game, laughing at what should grieve him. For a man of understanding, wisdom holds that place instead, so what each one takes pleasure in shows which way he walks.
23.explain:
“To do evil is like sport to a fool,”

Sport here is laughter or play. The fool treats wrongdoing as a game, something to joke about and enjoy. He laughs at what should grieve him. Proverbs says elsewhere, “Fools mock at sin” (14:9). What a person finds funny shows what he thinks of sin.

“But a man of understanding has wisdom.”

The Hebrew line is brief and leaves the comparison unstated; it reads literally, and wisdom to a man of understanding. It implies that wisdom holds for the man of understanding the place that evil holds for the fool: his delight and his pleasure. The contrast is not only between two kinds of action but between two kinds of enjoyment. What a person takes pleasure in reveals which way he walks.
23.notes:
Several versions fill out the compressed second line. The ESV makes wisdom the man of understanding’s “pleasure,” and the NASB supplies words so that wisdom is his “sport” as evil is the fool’s. The NLT has “living wisely brings pleasure to the sensible.”

The Hebrew noun behind “sport” means laughter or play. It comes from the same root as the verb translated “Rejoicing” in 8:30–31, where Wisdom delights before the LORD. The fool finds that kind of delight in doing evil.

24.brief: The wicked will meet the very thing they dread, while the righteous will receive what they desire. Each finally comes face to face with what was in his heart all along, the wicked with fear realized and the righteous with longing fulfilled.
24.explain:
“The fear of the wicked will come upon him,”

This “fear” is not the fear of the LORD. It is what the wicked man dreads: disaster, exposure, loss, and judgment. He lives with a dread he tries to ignore, and the saying warns that what he fears will come. Wisdom warned the scoffers in the same way: “When your terror comes like a storm” (1:27).

“And the desire of the righteous will be granted.”

The righteous also look ahead, but with longing rather than dread, and their desire will be granted. Each person finally meets what was in his heart all along. The saying speaks of the desire of a heart set on God, not every wish a righteous person might have. Psalm 37:4 puts it this way: “Delight yourself also in the LORD, And He shall give you the desires of your heart.” Like the sayings around it, this describes how the two ways end.
24.notes: The word for “fear” here is a different Hebrew word from the one in “the fear of the LORD” (10:27). The ESV renders it with the verb “dreads.”

25.brief: When the storm sweeps through, the wicked are gone like debris in a whirlwind. The righteous remain standing because they rest on a foundation that lasts forever, a picture Jesus echoes in the house built on the rock (Matthew 7:24–25).
25.explain:
“When the whirlwind passes by, the wicked is no more,”

The whirlwind is a sudden, violent storm. When it sweeps through, the wicked are gone like debris carried off by the wind. Wisdom used the same picture when she warned that destruction would come “like a whirlwind” (1:27). The wicked man may look secure, but he has nothing to hold him when the storm comes.

“But the righteous has an everlasting foundation.”

The righteous are not promised that no storm will come, or that a storm will never take their possessions or even their lives. Righteous people do suffer loss, and they die. What the verse promises is that the storm cannot sweep them away as it sweeps away the wicked, because they rest on a foundation that lasts. Their final security is the same one 10:30 states: “The righteous will never be removed.” Jesus used the same picture when He described the wise man whose house stood: “the winds blew and beat on that house; and it did not fall, for it was founded on the rock” (Matthew 7:25). The difference between the two is not the storm but what each one stands on.
25.notes: The Hebrew line has no verb; it reads literally, and a righteous one, a foundation forever. The KJV reads it as saying that the righteous person himself is an everlasting foundation. The NKJV takes the line as describing what he has, while the ESV and the 1984 NIV express the result, that he is established or stands firm forever.

26.brief: Vinegar sets the teeth on edge and smoke stings the eyes, and the lazy man irritates those who send him on an errand in the same way. Here laziness is seen from the side of the people who depend on him and are let down.
26.explain:
“As vinegar to the teeth and smoke to the eyes,”

Two small irritations from daily life make the point. Vinegar, sour wine, sets the teeth on edge, and smoke from a fire stings the eyes. Neither is a disaster, but both are unpleasant and hard to ignore.

“So is the lazy man to those who send him.”

The lazy man is the sluggard first described in 6:6–11. Here he is seen from the side of the people who depend on him. Someone sends him on an errand or trusts him with a task, and he delays, forgets, or does it halfway. His employer is left irritated and let down. Laziness is not a private weakness; it affects everyone who relies on the lazy person. The saying is about unwillingness, not about the limits of someone who is ill or unable.
26.notes:
This is the chapter’s only comparison of the “As … So” kind; the other sayings are mostly contrasts.

A later saying shows the opposite picture: “a faithful messenger to those who send him” refreshes his masters “Like the cold of snow in time of harvest” (25:13).

27.brief: Living in the fear of the LORD, a right view of God, tends to lengthen life, while the years of the wicked are cut short. This is the general pattern of God’s world, not a rule that explains every early death.
27.explain:
“The fear of the LORD prolongs days,”

The fear of the LORD is a right view of God, awe at His holiness and a heart that turns from evil. Living that way tends to lengthen life. It keeps a person from the violence, excess, and reckless choices that cut lives short. Wisdom said the same thing in 9:11: “For by me your days will be multiplied.”

“But the years of the wicked will be shortened.”

The wicked shorten their own years by the way they live, and God’s order in the world works against them. This is the general pattern of God’s world, not a rule that explains every death. Godly people sometimes die young, and wicked people sometimes live long. Jesus, who had all wisdom, did not live a long life. The saying must never be used to judge someone who has died early or to wound a family that is grieving.
27.notes:
The Hebrew verb behind “prolongs” means adds. The 1611 King James Version points this out in its margin, giving the Hebrew as “addeth,” and it is the same verb used when Wisdom says years of life “will be added” (9:11).

The LORD is named four times in this chapter (10:3, 22, 27, 29), each time in a saying about outcomes.

28.brief: Hope held by the righteous will end in gladness. The wicked are also looking forward to something, but what they expect will perish, because it was never anchored in God.
28.explain:
“The hope of the righteous will be gladness,”

Hope is confident expectation. The righteous look forward to what God will do, and their hope ends in joy. The Hebrew has no verb in this line, so it can also be read “is gladness”: the hope itself is already a source of joy, not only its fulfillment.

“But the expectation of the wicked will perish.”

The wicked also expect things. They count on their plans, their gains, and their schemes, but what they expect will perish. Proverbs says it again: “When a wicked man dies, his expectation will perish” (11:7). The difference lies in what each hope rests on. The hope of the righteous is anchored in God, while the hope of the wicked rests on things that do not last.

29.brief: One and the same way of the LORD has two effects. To the upright it gives strength, but for those who work iniquity it brings destruction, because God’s way does not bend to suit them.
29.explain:
“The way of the LORD is strength for the upright,”

“The way of the LORD” is God’s way of ordering life and dealing with people. To the upright it is strength, a place of safety and power to keep going. Those who walk in step with God’s way find that it holds them up.

“But destruction will come to the workers of iniquity.”

The same way of the LORD brings ruin to those who practice evil. God’s way does not change to suit them; they collide with it. The prophet Hosea ends his book with the same truth: “For the ways of the LORD are right; The righteous walk in them, But transgressors stumble in them” (Hosea 14:9). One and the same way is strength for some and destruction for others, depending on how a person walks.
29.notes: The Hebrew word translated “strength” means a place or means of safety, a refuge or stronghold. The ESV, NASB, and NLT render it “stronghold.”

30.brief: The righteous will never be uprooted, while the wicked will not remain in the earth. The saying looks to how the two ways finally end, with the righteous secure and the wicked removed, rather than promising that the righteous never suffer loss.
30.explain:
“The righteous will never be removed,”

To be removed is to be shaken loose, uprooted, or moved from one’s place. The righteous will not be uprooted. Their stability comes from God, who keeps them. This does not mean they never face hardship or loss; it means they will not finally be torn out of the place God gives them.

“But the wicked will not inhabit the earth.”

The wicked will not remain. In Israel’s setting, dwelling in the land was the gift God gave His people, and the father had already said, “the upright will dwell in the land,” while “the wicked will be cut off from the earth” (2:21–22). The saying looks to how the two ways finally end. It is not a promise that the righteous never lose a home or that the wicked never prosper for a time.
30.notes:
The Hebrew word for “earth” here is also the ordinary word for “land,” and the ESV renders it “the land.” The NKJV of 2:21–22 uses both English words for it.

Proverbs 10:31–32 — The Mouth of the Righteous Brings Forth Wisdom

31.brief: Like a healthy plant bearing fruit, the mouth of the righteous brings forth wisdom. The perverse tongue, twisted and deceitful, will be cut out like a branch that bears nothing good.
31.explain:
“The mouth of the righteous brings forth wisdom,”

The Hebrew verb translated “brings forth” pictures a plant bearing fruit. Wisdom grows out of the mouth of the righteous naturally, the way fruit grows on a healthy tree. Their speech is not a performance; it is the fruit of what is in them.

“But the perverse tongue will be cut out.”

The perverse tongue is twisted, turning things upside down and bending truth into deceit. It “will be cut out,” like a branch that bears nothing good. The two lines continue the plant picture: one mouth bears fruit, the other tongue is cut off. After so many sayings about words, the chapter returns to them at the end.
31.notes: The Hebrew verb behind “brings forth” is a poetic word that means to bear fruit. It is used of the righteous as fruitful trees in Psalm 92:14, “They shall still bear fruit in old age.” Its meaning supports the plant picture of this verse, in which one mouth bears fruit and the other tongue is cut off like a useless branch. The NASB renders it “flows.”

32.brief: Righteous lips know what is fitting and welcome to say, so their words build up. The mouth of the wicked knows only what is perverse, and the chapter closes on the conviction that speech reveals which way a person walks.
32.explain:
“The lips of the righteous know what is acceptable,”

What is “acceptable” is what is fitting, welcome, and pleasing. The righteous know what to say and when to say it. Their words build up, because they have learned to speak in a way that pleases God and helps people.

“But the mouth of the wicked what is perverse.”

The verb carries over from the first line: the mouth of the wicked “knows” only what is perverse, twisted, and contrary. It is skilled in the wrong things. With this pair of sayings, 10:31–32, the chapter ends where so much of it has dwelt, on speech. A person’s mouth shows which way he walks.
32.notes:
The Hebrew word for “acceptable” means goodwill, favor, or what pleases. Here it describes words that are welcome and fitting to those who hear them. In 11:1 the same word is translated “His delight,” where a just weight pleases the LORD.

The Hebrew word translated “perverse” is the same in 10:31 and 10:32, linking the two verses and closing the chapter with a matched pair of sayings.
